Shekel Plunge Sparks Economic Turmoil Across Israel as Companies Feel the Pinch

Israel is grappling with escalating economic turmoil this week after a sharp and unexpected collapse in the value of the shekel sent shockwaves through its financial markets and real economy. The currency, which has lost over 20% of its value against the US dollar in just two weeks, is at its lowest level since 2002, sparking fears of a broader financial crisis.

Businesses and households alike are feeling the impact. Import costs have surged, with prices for fuel and key raw materials climbing steeply. The Bank of Israel has intervened twice in the past week, selling reserves in an attempt to stabilize the currency, but so far with limited effect.

Industrial energy providers are among the hardest hit. Dalia Power Energies Ltd, one of the country’s largest independent electricity producers, confirmed on Thursday that its operational costs had risen sharply as a result of the shekel’s fall. “Most of our fuel contracts are denominated in dollars,” said a company spokesperson. “The sudden increase in expenses is forcing us to review our pricing and operations daily.”

Other sectors are also reeling. The National Retailers Association warned that food and consumer goods prices could rise by as much as 15% in the coming month if the shekel does not recover. Meanwhile, the Israeli Manufacturers Union called for emergency government assistance, citing threats to jobs and export competitiveness.

Economists are divided on how long the crisis might last. “If confidence is not restored quickly, we could see capital flight and even higher inflation,” said Dr. Yael Shapiro, an economics lecturer at Tel Aviv University.

The Prime Minister’s office released a brief statement urging calm and promising “decisive steps to restore financial stability.” As the shekel continues its volatile slide, many Israelis remain anxious about what the coming weeks will bring.
